opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I think the Continuous Thought Machine is worth paying attention to mainly because it's a genuine attempt to step outside the current paradigm, and honestly there aren't many of those right now. Since the transformer came out, and I say this as one of the people who worked on it, the field has converged hard. Almost everyone is iterating on the same architecture: scaling it, tweaking it, finding better ways to train it. That's produced amazing results, but it also means we've stopped exploring.

With the CTM, we took inspiration from biology. Not in a slavish "let's simulate the brain" way, but by asking what modern neural networks threw away for convenience. The big one is time. Real neurons have dynamics; their timing matters, and they synchronize with each other. In a standard network, a neuron is just a number passed through a nonlinearity. So in the CTM each neuron has its own small model that processes a history of its incoming signals, and the representation the model actually uses is the synchronization between neurons over time. And the model has an internal "thinking" dimension that's decoupled from the input, so it can take as many internal steps as it needs.

What excited us is what emerged from that. On maze solving, you can watch the attention trace a path through the maze, step by step, almost like it's planning a route. On image classification, it looks around the image in a very human-like way. And we get adaptive computation essentially for free: on easy examples it becomes confident quickly and can stop, and on hard ones it keeps thinking. We didn't have to bolt that on with some special loss term; it falls out of the design.

I don't want to oversell it. It isn't going to replace transformers tomorrow. But I think research is in a slightly unhealthy place where everything has to beat a benchmark immediately, or it's not worth publishing. The CTM is more of a statement: there are still interesting, unexplored directions, and if we give ourselves the freedom to follow curiosity, we might find the next big thing rather than just the next incremental improvement. That's really why I think people should pay attention to it.

r001.rationale: The response says the CTM gets adaptive computation from its design: it stops on easy examples and keeps thinking on hard ones.

r002.rationale: It describes each neuron's model processing a history of incoming signals and says the representation the model uses is synchronization between neurons over time, communicating synchronization as the representation in its iterative model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that excites me most about it is that it's a bet on something the field has basically stopped betting on, which is that the way neurons compute actually matters.

If you look at where we are, the dominant architecture, the Transformer, works incredibly well, and I had a hand in that, so I'm not going to complain too loudly. But the neuron inside it is still essentially the 1950s neuron: a weighted sum and a nonlinearity. And one thing we've thrown away, almost on purpose because it made things easier to scale, is time. Biological neurons don't just output a number, they fire in patterns, and the timing of those firings relative to each other carries information. Synchronisation is how real brains seem to bind things together, and we've completely ignored it in deep learning.

So the Continuous Thought Machine does two things that I think are genuinely different. First, every neuron has its own little model that looks at a history of its inputs rather than just the current one, so neurons get to have temporal dynamics. And second, the representation the model actually uses to act isn't the activations themselves, it's the synchronisation between neurons over time. That's the thing you read out from. That's a pretty radical change in what a "representation" even means.

And the reason I think it's worth paying attention to, rather than just being a cute neuroscience-flavoured idea, is what you see when you watch it work. It has an internal clock that's decoupled from the data, so it can take as many ticks as it wants to think about an input. When you give it a maze, you can literally watch the attention trace the path. When you give it an image, it looks around, saccades almost, and it's more confident on easy examples and spends longer on hard ones, without us ever telling it to do that. Adaptive compute just falls out of the dynamics. That's the kind of behaviour we've been trying to bolt onto Transformers with chain of thought and all sorts of scaffolding, and here it emerges from the architecture.

Now, I want to be careful. It's not going to beat a frontier language model tomorrow, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who told you it would. The point at Sakana isn't to win the benchmark today, it's to explore parts of the design space that the industry has decided aren't worth the trouble because they don't scale neatly on a GPU yet. And I think there's a real risk in the field right now that we've converged so hard on one recipe that we've forgotten there are other recipes. The CTM is interesting to me precisely because it's a reminder that intelligence might not be only about scale. It might also be about dynamics, and we've barely started looking there.

r001.rationale: It describes adaptive computation emerging from the model’s dynamics: the model can take more ticks and spends longer on harder examples without being instructed to do so.

r002.rationale: It says the model represents information through synchronization between neurons over time, alongside neurons with temporal dynamics based on input history.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s worth paying attention to because it asks whether we’ve made the right assumptions about how neural networks should compute. In a lot of our models, you put an input in and it passes through a fixed sequence of layers. There isn’t much freedom for the model to spend time working on something.

The Continuous Thought Machine makes that internal time dimension central. Neurons have a history of activity, and the model uses how their activity synchronizes over time as a representation. So computation becomes an evolving process, and you can look at what happens as the system takes more steps.

That opens up some interesting questions. Can a model spend more computation on a difficult example? Can useful intermediate behaviour emerge without us prescribing every step? I wouldn’t take the results as proof that this is the next dominant architecture. What excites me is that it’s a concrete, testable alternative to assumptions we’ve become very comfortable with.

r001.rationale: It presents spending more computation on a difficult example as an interesting possibility enabled by the model’s central internal time dimension.

r002.rationale: It clearly says activity synchronization over time serves as a representation, but does not clearly identify the model as recurrent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is whether we’ve chosen the right abstraction for computation in neural networks. We tend to think in terms of layers: you put an input in, push it through a fixed amount of computation, and get an answer. But why should every problem need the same amount of thought?

The Continuous Thought Machine explores a different approach, where computation unfolds over internal time, and the temporal behaviour of neurons matters. In particular, it uses synchronisation between neurons as part of its representation. That gives you a different way to think about how a network develops an answer, rather than just making the network deeper.

What makes that worth paying attention to, for me, is the possibility of more flexible computation. A system could spend longer on something difficult, and you can examine how its predictions evolve as it thinks. That doesn’t mean it’s automatically better, or that borrowing an idea from biology makes it correct. It means there’s a genuinely different architectural hypothesis to test. And I think we need more of those.

r001.rationale: It describes flexible computation in which a system can spend longer on difficult problems, communicating adaptive computation as a reason to consider the model.

r002.rationale: It says synchronization between neurons is part of the representation, but does not identify the model as recurrent.
